newsitem.title: UK: Who's afraid of derivative losses? Managers are.
newsitem.headline: Who's afraid of derivative losses? Managers are.

text.p: As National Westminster Bank plc planned on Thursday to claw back bonuses and suspended senior staff, London's financial community saw signs of added rigour in the trend to make management pay for derivatives disasters.
Many in the markets said it was about time too.
They said the current generation of management has never really got to grips with the complexities involved in trading esoteric instruments in options and other derivatives markets.

"Most of the blokes in charge wouldn't know the difference between a put and a call if one came up and bit them," said one broker. "They don't know enough to ask the right questions. If an options trade looks too good to be true, it probably is."

NatWest on Thursday said its multi-million pound interest rate options losses totalled 90 million pounds ($140 million) -- nearly double the 50 million total it revealed last month when it announced it was taking a charge for options mispricing errors.

Five NatWest staff have been suspended, and eight million pounds in bonuses have been withheld. Among those suspended were the global head of options, global head of rate risk management and a chief administrative officer.
The trader believed to be at the bottom of the whole affair, Kyriakos Papouis, left NatWest last year and has since resigned from the bank he went to, Bear Stearns.

Although senior managers have had to fall on their swords following trading debacles such as the collapse of Barings and the Sumitomo copper scandal, the public relations battle was always initially to try to lay the blame on lone "rogue" individuals.
"With Barings and Sumitomo, it was very much a case of pinning everything on one trader," said the manager of an options desk on the floor of LIFFE, Europe's busiest derivatives exchange.

Traders noted that Nick Leeson, the so-called rogue trader who caused the collapse of Barings in 1995 under the weight of 800 million pounds of unauthorised derivatives trading, was portrayed as the sole cause of the disaster.
Similarly, Yasuo Hamanaka, Sumitomo's copper trading chief who lost $2.6 billion -- the largest ever in a financial market -- was also painted as bearing the responsibility alone.

"The bottom line is that the senior guys are willing to take the credit when the derivatives profits are rolling in, but they're not so visible when things turn the other way," said a dealer of British interest rate futures.
The options manager on LIFFE said the level of expertise in senior management did not reflect the degree of complexity in the market.

But traders said financial institutions were increasingly unhappy about the image that such large-scale losses were engendering, and would not tolerate constantly being dragged through the mud of bad publicity.
"If they can put the frighteners on people, making it known that they are responsible for their staff, it might make a difference," said a German government bond trader.

Market players said the general feeling among traders was that more experience was needed among both senior and back office staff in spotting "holes" or anomalies in complicated financial instruments.
